author: Biography of Srinivasa Ramanujan
prose_text_en: The biography recounts Srinivasa Ramanujan's life, starting with a classroom anecdote where he questioned division by zero, proposing the answer as infinity. Ramanujan, a child prodigy from Erode (born Dec 22, 1887), mastered S.L. Loney’s advanced trigonometry and G.S. Carr’s 'A Synopsis of Elementary Results in Pure Applied Mathematics'. Despite his genius, he struggled with formal education, failing college exams due to neglecting other subjects. He eventually secured a clerk position at Madras Port Trust through Francis Spring. His path-breaking letter to G.H. Hardy at Cambridge led to his fellowship at Trinity College. He contributed significantly to number theory (Partition Theory, modular equations, and the Hardy-Ramanujan-Littlewood circle method). He passed away young, following a battle with Tuberculosis.
summary_en: Srinivasa Ramanujan was an extraordinary Indian mathematical genius who rose from humble beginnings to international acclaim despite a lack of formal training. His work in number theory, particularly his Partition Theory, continues to influence modern technology, including ATM functionality. Though he faced early rejection and poor health, his dedication to mathematics led him to become the first Indian Fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge.
